question: Give an example of receiving critical or tough feedback. How did you respond?

raiseTranscript.text: My manager said my PRs had too many bugs and unclear variable names. I felt embarrassed but asked for specific examples.
I rewrote the next two features with better naming and added unit tests. My bug rate dropped and he noted it in the next 1:1.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of receiving critical or tough feedback. How did you respond?
Role: new engineer on payments service
Situation: manager flagged buggy PRs and poor naming
Action: asked for examples, rewrote two features with tests
Outcome: bug rate dropped, positive note in 1:1
Quote: 'I felt embarrassed but asked for specific examples'
Follow-up: How did you feel initially? -> Owned it and iterated
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. Candidate described receiving direct feedback on code quality and variable naming. They asked for specifics then rewrote two features with added tests, resulting in lower bug rate noted by manager. This shows coachability and ownership of individual output. The story stays local to their work and demonstrates quick application of feedback without defensiveness. Biggest strength is treating the feedback as actionable rather than personal.

lowerTranscript.text: My manager said my code had bugs. I explained why the approach was correct given the deadline.
Did anything change after that conversation?
Not really, the project shipped and I moved on to the next task.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of receiving critical or tough feedback. How did you respond?
Role: new engineer on payments service
Situation: manager flagged buggy PRs
Action: defended the approach citing deadline pressure
Outcome: no change, moved to next task
Quote: 'I explained why the approach was correct given the deadline'
Follow-up: Did anything change? -> Nothing, project shipped
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. Candidate received feedback on buggy code but responded by justifying the work instead of addressing the issues. No follow-up actions were taken and the behavior did not change. The story shows limited ownership and weak response to direct input on their output. This signals low coachability at the individual contributor level. Biggest gap is absence of any learning or adjustment after the feedback.

raiseTranscript.text: A peer team lead told me my design doc for the new API ignored latency requirements from their service.
I scheduled a joint review, updated the doc with their numbers, and added a fallback path. Two other teams later reused the pattern.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of receiving critical or tough feedback. How did you respond?
Role: senior on checkout platform
Situation: peer lead flagged missing latency requirements in design
Action: scheduled joint review, revised doc, added fallback
Outcome: two other teams reused the updated pattern
Quote: 'I scheduled a joint review, updated the doc with their numbers'
Follow-up: What was the cross-team result? -> Pattern adopted elsewhere
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. Candidate received direct feedback from a peer team on an API design missing latency needs. They organized a joint review, incorporated the data, and added a fallback that later became reusable by two other teams. The response shows influence without authority and measurable cross-team impact. Story stays grounded in technical work with clear follow-through. Biggest strength is turning critical input into a pattern others adopted.

lowerTranscript.text: A peer team lead said my API design missed their latency needs. I added a note in the doc but kept the main path the same.
Did the other team adopt it?
They built their own version instead.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of receiving critical or tough feedback. How did you respond?
Role: senior on checkout platform
Situation: peer lead flagged missing latency in design
Action: added a note but kept original path unchanged
Outcome: peer team built their own solution
Quote: 'I added a note in the doc but kept the main path the same'
Follow-up: Did the other team adopt it? -> No, they built separately
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. Candidate received feedback on an API design but only added a note without changing the core approach. The peer team ended up building their own solution. This shows limited influence and minimal adjustment despite cross-team input. The story lacks evidence of driving alignment or broader impact. Biggest gap is treating feedback as documentation rather than a signal to iterate.

raiseTranscript.text: My skip-level told me my team was missing promotion cases because I was not coaching on impact writing.
I started bi-weekly calibration sessions, had each engineer draft their own promo doc, and three people were promoted in the next cycle.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of receiving critical or tough feedback. How did you respond?
Role: engineering manager of 8
Situation: skip-level flagged weak promotion cases due to poor coaching
Action: ran bi-weekly calibration, had engineers draft their docs
Outcome: three promotions in next cycle
Quote: 'I started bi-weekly calibration sessions'
Follow-up: How did the team respond? -> Engineers owned their narratives
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. Candidate received feedback that their team lacked strong promotion cases due to insufficient coaching on impact. They introduced bi-weekly calibration sessions and required engineers to draft their own documents, resulting in three promotions. The response demonstrates developing the team and owning team-level outcomes. Story focuses on process change with measurable people results. Biggest strength is converting personal feedback into leverage for multiple team members.

lowerTranscript.text: My skip-level said my team was weak on promotion cases. I told the team to work on their impact statements.
One person was promoted but the others stayed flat.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of receiving critical or tough feedback. How did you respond?
Role: engineering manager of 8
Situation: skip-level flagged weak promotion cases
Action: told team to work on impact statements
Outcome: only one promotion, others flat
Quote: 'I told the team to work on their impact statements'
Follow-up: Did promotion rates improve? -> Minimal change
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. Candidate received feedback on weak team promotion cases but responded with a one-time directive rather than structured coaching. Only one promotion occurred afterward. This shows limited ownership of team development and weak follow-through on people outcomes. The story lacks evidence of creating leverage or addressing underperformance in skill building. Biggest gap is absence of sustained process change after the feedback.

raiseTranscript.text: The CEO told me our org was losing senior talent because leaders were not owning retention conversations.
I created a quarterly retention review with each director, tied it to their performance goals, and reduced senior attrition from 18% to 9% over 18 months.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of receiving critical or tough feedback. How did you respond?
Role: VP Engineering
Situation: CEO flagged high senior attrition due to weak leader ownership
Action: launched quarterly retention reviews tied to director goals
Outcome: senior attrition dropped from 18% to 9% in 18 months
Quote: 'I created a quarterly retention review with each director'
Follow-up: How did you measure success? -> 18% to 9% attrition
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. Candidate received direct feedback from the CEO on senior talent loss tied to leader behavior. They introduced quarterly retention reviews linked to director performance goals, cutting attrition from 18% to 9% over 18 months. The response shows strategic judgment and org-level impact with clear long-term metrics. Story demonstrates creating systemic leverage rather than heroics. Biggest strength is translating blunt feedback into a durable process that improved retention at scale.

lowerTranscript.text: The CEO said we were losing seniors because leaders avoided hard retention talks. I sent an email reminding directors to have stay conversations.
What was the result on attrition?
It stayed roughly the same the following year.

lowerNotes: Q: Give an example of receiving critical or tough feedback. How did you respond?
Role: VP Engineering
Situation: CEO flagged high senior attrition
Action: sent email reminder about stay conversations
Outcome: attrition unchanged the next year
Quote: 'I sent an email reminding directors to have stay conversations'
Follow-up: What was the result on attrition? -> Stayed the same
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. Candidate received feedback on senior attrition but responded with a single email rather than structural change. Attrition remained flat the following year. This shows limited strategic judgment and weak ownership of org-level outcomes. The story lacks evidence of long-term thinking or creating leverage through leaders. Biggest gap is treating a business-critical signal as a communication task instead of a systemic issue.
